walkthroughs.body_html:
Sociology Basics: Key Concepts & Processes — a core area of GCSE Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Sociology Basics: Key Concepts & Processes brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Sociology Basics: Key Concepts & Processes.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Who argued the family had become symmetrical in 1973?
options: Murdock
Parsons
Young and Willmott
Oakley

mcqs.q: Murdock (1949) identified how many family functions?
What do feminists mean by the 'dark side' of family life?
options: The 'dark side' is a metaphor about families who don't communicate.
The 'dark side' refers to families who live in poverty.
A self-fulfilling prophecy is when teachers predict the future accurately.

The reality that families can be sites of inequality, exploitation and violence — particularly affecting women and children — challenging functionalist portrayals of the family as universally beneficial.

mcqs.q: What is the Marxist view on white-collar crime?
options: The 'dark side' is a metaphor about families who don't communicate.
It is widespread but under-policed because law serves ruling-class interests.
It is treated more harshly than street crime.
It does not really happen - only the working class commit crime.

mcqs.q: What is a self-fulfilling prophecy in education?
options: It is treated more harshly than street crime.
A self-fulfilling prophecy is when a student predicts their own grade correctly.
A self-fulfilling prophecy is when teachers predict the future accurately.

When teachers' expectations (often based on labels) influence pupil behaviour and achievement — pupils labelled as 'bright' tend to do better, those labelled 'thick' worse, regardless of underlying ability (Rosenthal and Jacobson).
